summary: Describes how to test and measure the performance of devices that forward IP multicast traffic. It builds on earlier benchmarking methodology work such as RFC 2544 and extends it from one-to-one traffic to one-to-many traffic. It is a methodology guide for testers, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3918 is a testing manual for routers that forward IP multicast. It says how to wire up the test, which frame sizes to use, how long to run each trial, and how to measure how much traffic the device can copy to many receivers, how long a packet takes to come out, and how long it takes to start and stop sending to a group.

questions: how do igmp group changes affect device performance
how is latency measured in multicast routing
subtitle: A step-by-step method for measuring how well a router forwards one-to-many IP traffic

tldr.problem: Benchmarking rules existed for one-to-one traffic, but a device that copies one packet to many destinations behaves differently, and there was no agreed way to measure it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo extends the earlier benchmarking work to the multicast case, giving a test set-up, then a procedure for each measurement: throughput, forwarding latency, the delay in joining and leaving a group, group capacity, and the same measurements taken while the device is busy with other traffic.
tldr.outcome: Each procedure states the objective, the steps, and what the report must contain, so that results from different testers can be compared. The memo is a method for measurement, not a protocol, and it says so.

today: RFC 3918 is an Informational memo from October 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a measurement methodology, not a protocol, and its security considerations section says there are no security considerations specific to the document, while warning that results obtained in a test context might not be representative of the same device in an operational network.

sections.title: What This Memo Measures
sections.content:
This document defines tests for measuring and reporting the throughput, forwarding, latency and Internet Group Management Protocol group membership characteristics of devices that support IP multicast protocols. The results of these tests provide the user with meaningful data on multicast performance.

A previous document, Terminology for IP Multicast Benchmarking, defined many of the terms used here, and the terminology document should be consulted before making use of this one. The methodology builds on the tenets set forth in RFC 2544, RFC 2432 and other efforts of the IETF Benchmarking Methodology Working Group, and seeks to extend them to the multicast paradigm. The working group produces two major classes of documents: Terminology documents that present the benchmarks and other related terms, and Methodology documents that define the procedures required to collect the benchmarks cited in the corresponding terminology document.

The methodology focuses on one source to many destinations, although many of the tests described may be extended to use multiple source to multiple destination topologies. Subsequent documents may address IPv6 multicast and related multicast routing protocol performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Existing test methods covered traffic sent to one place. This one covers the harder case, where a single packet is copied out to many receivers, and says exactly how to run each test so that two laboratories get comparable numbers.

sections.title: Setting Up the Test
sections.content:
The methodologies are for single ingress, multiple egress multicast scenarios. Methodologies for multiple ingress and multiple egress scenarios are beyond the scope of the document. The typical setup has a source test port feeding one ingress interface of the device under test, and the device forwarding out of several egress interfaces to destination test ports. If the metrics are taken across multiple devices forming a system under test, test frames are offered to a single ingress interface on a device of the system, forwarded across the system topology, and finally forwarded to the test apparatus by the test egress interfaces of devices in the system. If a system is tested, the test topology and all relevant configuration details must be disclosed with the corresponding test results.

Generally, the destination test ports first join the desired number of multicast groups by sending IGMP Group Report messages to the device. To verify that all destination test ports successfully joined the appropriate groups, the source test port must transmit IP multicast frames destined for these groups. After test completion, the destination test ports may send IGMP Leave Group messages to clear the IGMP table of the device. Test equipment must also validate the correct and proper forwarding actions of the devices it tests, to ensure the receipt of the frames involved in the test.

The methodology assumes a uniform medium topology, and issues such as mixed transmission media, speed mismatch and header differences are not specifically addressed. Flow control, quality of service and other non-essential traffic or traffic-affecting mechanisms affecting the variable under test must be disabled, and any modifications to the collection procedures needed to accommodate the media actually tested must be presented with the results. An actual flow of test traffic may be required to prime related mechanisms, such as processing reverse path forwarding events and building device caches, so that subsequent traffic is forwarded optimally. The test apparatus must therefore generate test traffic with the same addressing characteristics before any test that forwards multicast or unicast packets, and the priming action need only be repeated to keep the associated information current. The memo notes that the formation of the multicast distribution tree may be a significant component of multicast performance, but it does not seek to benchmark that, leaving it as future work specific to a given tree formation vehicle.

On the details that matter for repeatability: all of the ingress and egress interfaces must support a version of IGMP, and the IGMP version on the ingress interface must be the same version being tested on the egress interfaces. Each interface should be able to respond to IGMP queries during the test, and should also send a LEAVE, running IGMP version 2 or later, after each test. There is no restriction on the use of multicast addresses other than the assignments imposed by IANA, which must be regarded for operational consistency, and address selection does not need to be restricted to administratively scoped addresses. Each test should be run with different multicast frame sizes, and for Ethernet the recommended sizes are 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280 and 1518 byte frames; other link layer technologies may be used, in which case the minimum and maximum frame lengths of the technology in use should be tested, and the device configuration must remain the same when the frame size changes. The data plane test traffic should have a TTL large enough to traverse the device, while the TTL in IGMP control plane messages must comply with the version of IGMP in use. The duration of the test portion of each trial should be at least 30 seconds, and this parameter must be included in the results reporting for each methodology.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving ports announce themselves to the device with IGMP, and the tester checks they really joined by sending traffic to those groups. Everything else is switched off that might change the result, and each trial runs for at least 30 seconds.

sections.title: Forwarding and Throughput
sections.content:
This section describes the tests related to the characterization of frame forwarding in a multicast environment. Some metrics extend the concept of throughput presented in RFC 1242, and forwarding rate is cited in RFC 2285.

Mixed Class Throughput determines the throughput of a device when both unicast class frames and multicast class frames are offered simultaneously to a fixed number of interfaces. Multicast and unicast traffic are mixed in the same aggregated traffic stream to simulate a heterogeneous networking environment. Before test traffic is offered, all destination test ports configured to receive multicast traffic must join all configured multicast groups, the device must learn the appropriate unicast and multicast addresses, and group membership and unicast address learning must be verified through some externally observable method. The intended load should be configured as alternating multicast class frames and unicast class frames to a single ingress interface, with the unicast class frames configured to transmit in an unweighted round-robin fashion to all of the destination ports. The example given uses six multicast groups and 3 destination ports with one unicast address per port, and the source test port offers frames in the order m1 u1 m2 u2 m3 u3 m4 u1 m5 u2 m6 u3 m1 and so on, where m is a multicast frame for a group and u is a unicast frame for a target port. A search algorithm must be used to determine the mixed class throughput, and the ratio of unicast to multicast frames must remain the same when varying the intended load. The report must reflect the frame sizes, the number of tested egress interfaces, the test duration, the IGMP version, the total number of multicast groups, the traffic distribution for both classes and the ratio between them, and must state the mixed class throughput including the throughput per class.

The Scaled Group Forwarding Matrix determines the forwarding rate as a function of the number of multicast groups tested, for a fixed number of tested ports. It is iterative: the destination test ports join an initial number of groups, recommended as 10 groups, multicast traffic is transmitted to all of them and the forwarding rate is measured. The number of groups is then incremented by a further number, with a recommended granularity of 10 groups per iteration, though a finer granularity may be chosen, and the measurement is repeated. The total number of groups joined must not exceed the multicast group capacity of the device, so the group capacity results must be known before running the test. The report must show the total number of groups joined and the forwarding rate for each iteration.

Aggregated Multicast Throughput determines the maximum rate at which none of the offered frames are dropped through N destination interfaces of the same multicast groups. Traffic is offered at an initial maximum offered load to a fixed set of interfaces, with a fixed number of groups, a fixed frame length and a fixed duration. If any frame loss is detected the offered load is decreased and the sender transmits again, and an iterative search algorithm must be used to find the maximum offered frame rate with zero frame loss, varying the offered load while keeping the set of interfaces, number of groups, frame length and duration fixed.

Three further tests cover tunnelling, where a device wraps packets in another protocol on one side and unwraps them on the other. Encapsulation Throughput finds the maximum rate at which frames offered to one ingress interface are encapsulated and correctly forwarded on one or more egress interfaces without loss, with one or more tunnels created between each egress interface and a destination test port. Decapsulation Throughput finds the maximum rate at which frames offered to one ingress interface are decapsulated and correctly forwarded, with one or more tunnels between the source test port and the device. Re-encapsulation Throughput finds the maximum rate at which frames of one encapsulated format are converted to another encapsulated format and correctly forwarded. In each case the number of multicast groups per tunnel must be the same when the device is configured with multiple tunnels, all destination test ports must join all multicast group addresses offered, and each egress interface must be configured with the same MTU. When offering large frame sizes, the encapsulation process may require the device to fragment the IP datagrams before forwarding, so it is recommended to limit the offered frame size so that no fragmentation is required. A search algorithm must be used to determine each of the three throughputs, and the reports must state the tunnel configuration, the encapsulation format used, the frame sizes and the measured throughput.
sections.plainLanguage: Three throughput questions: how much can the device copy when the traffic is part unicast and part multicast, how much can it copy as more and more receivers join, and how much can it push through when it also has to wrap and unwrap the packets in tunnels.

sections.title: Forwarding Latency
sections.content:
This section presents the methodologies for characterizing the forwarding latency of a device in a multicast environment, extending the concept of latency characterization presented in RFC 2544. The offered load accompanying the latency-measured packet can affect the packet buffering of the device, which may in turn affect the measured latency, so this should be considered when selecting the intended load. RFC 1242 and RFC 2544 draw a distinction between device types, store and forward and bit-forwarding, and each type affects how latency is collected and presented.

Multicast Latency produces a set of measurements from a single multicast ingress interface through multiple egress interfaces of the same device, as provided for by the metric in RFC 2432. The procedure draws on the collection methodology for latency in RFC 2544. The trial duration should be 120 seconds, to be consistent with RFC 2544, and the nature of the measurement, store and forward or bit forwarding, must be associated with the trial and disclosed in the results report.

A test traffic stream is presented to the device, and it is recommended to offer traffic at the measured aggregated multicast throughput rate. At the midpoint of the trial, the test apparatus must inject a uniquely identifiable, tagged frame into the traffic being presented, and the frame generation timestamp, Timestamp A, reflecting the completion of the transmission of that frame, must be determined. The apparatus monitors the tested egress interfaces for the expected tagged frames and must record the time of successful detection of a tagged frame from each egress interface with a timestamp, Timestamp B. A set of Timestamp B values must be collected for all tested egress interfaces. A trial must be considered invalid if there are unexpected differences between intended load and offered load or between offered load and the resulting forwarding rates, if forwarded test frames are improperly formed or their header fields improperly manipulated, if required tagged frames are not forwarded on all expected egress interfaces, or if tagged frames are received more than 5 seconds after the cessation of test traffic by the source port.

The set of latency measurements, M, composed from each measurement taken from every ingress and tested egress interface pairing, is determined from a valid trial as the set of Timestamp B values minus Timestamp A for each tested egress interface. A more continuous profile may be built from a series of individual measurements. The report must state the frame sizes, the number of tested egress interfaces, the test duration, the IGMP version, the offered load and the total number of multicast groups, and must give the set of all latencies with their time units for the tested ingress and each tested egress interface. The time units must be uniform and of sufficient precision for the medium being tested, and the results should preserve the relationship of latency to ingress and egress interface for each multicast group, to assist in trending across trials.

The Min/Max Multicast Latency benchmark determines the difference between the maximum and the minimum latency measurement from the collected set. From the set M of individual forwarding latencies between ingress and egress port pairs, identify MAX(M) and MIN(M), and the result is MAX(M) minus MIN(M). It is reported with the same configuration parameters and, optionally, the full set of latencies.
sections.plainLanguage: To measure the delay, the tester marks one packet among the traffic, notes the time it left, and notes the time it turned up at each output port. The difference is the delay, and the gap between the fastest and slowest output shows how uneven the device is.

sections.title: Overhead: Joining and Leaving a Group
sections.content:
The Overhead section characterizes the delay associated with explicit operations in multicast environments, which in practice means the time it takes to start and stop sending to a group.

Group Join Delay is the time a device takes to start forwarding multicast frames from the moment a successful IGMP group membership report has been issued to it. The measurement may be influenced by the state of the Multicast Forwarding Database. In State 0, the database does not contain the multicast group address, and the delay includes the time the device requires to add the address and begin forwarding, which says how well the device handles new addresses. In State 1, the database already contains the address, and the delay includes the time to update the database with the newly joined nodes and begin forwarding to them, plus packet replication time, which says how well the device copes with adding a new user to an event already being broadcast.

Two methods are given. Method A assumes the database is in State 0 and uses only one ingress and one egress; before any group membership reports are sent, it must be verified by externally observable means that the destination test port is not currently a member of the group and that the database does not contain the address. Method B assumes the database is in State 1 and may use one or more egress ports; it must be verified that the database contains the address, and a single un-instrumented test port joins the group first to populate it. The methods may be used independently or together, and the method used must be specified in the report. To minimize variation in the delay calculation and the burden on the device, the test should be performed with one multicast group, and all destination test ports must join it.

Once verification is complete, multicast traffic for the group must be offered to the ingress interface before the device receives any group membership report messages, and it is recommended to offer it at the measured aggregated multicast throughput rate. The destination test port then sends one group membership report for the group. The join delay is the difference between the time the last bit of the report is sent and the time the first bit of the first valid multicast frame is forwarded on the egress interface. The report must state the frame sizes, the number of tested egress interfaces, the IGMP version, the total number of multicast groups, the offered load and the method used, and must give the group join delay time in microseconds per egress interface.

Group Leave Delay is the time a device takes to cease forwarding multicast frames after an IGMP Leave Group message has been successfully offered to it. Before any leave messages are sent, it must be verified that the destination test ports are currently members of the group, and if any of the egress interfaces do not forward validation multicast frames then the test is invalid. Multicast traffic for the group must be offered to the ingress interface before receipt or processing of any leave messages, again recommended at the measured aggregated multicast throughput rate, and each destination test port then sends one leave message. The leave delay is the difference between the time the last bit of the leave message is sent and the time the last bit of the last valid multicast frame is forwarded on the egress interface, and it is reported in microseconds per egress interface.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone joins a broadcast, how long before the device starts sending to them? And when they leave, how long before it stops? The memo gives two ways to measure the first, because the answer depends on whether the device already knew about that group.

sections.title: Capacity and Interaction
sections.content:
Multicast Group Capacity identifies the maximum number of multicast groups a device can support while still forwarding multicast frames to all of the groups registered to it. One or more destination test ports join an initial number of groups, and after a minimum delay as measured by the group join delay procedure, the source test ports must transmit to each group at a specified offered load. If at least one frame for each group is forwarded properly on each participating egress interface, the iteration passes at the current capacity. Each successful iteration is followed by the destination test ports joining an additional user-defined number of groups, and the test stops when an egress interface fails to forward traffic on one or more of the configured groups. The last successful iteration is the Maximum Group Capacity result, and the report must give the total number of group addresses successfully forwarded through the device.

Interaction covers the fact that network devices generally provide more functionality than forwarding, and may be asked to provide it in a variety of environments. The Forwarding Burdened Multicast Latency test follows the setup of the multicast latency test, and adds a set of burdening ports that transmit unicast class traffic to the device in a fully meshed distribution as described in RFC 2285. The device must learn the appropriate unicast addresses, verified through some externally observable method. A baseline measurement of multicast latency is taken first, then the unicast traffic is started at a user-specified offered load and the multicast latency test is rerun, with the same offered load to the ingress port as in the baseline. The report must give the latencies for both the baseline and the burdened response, along with the offered load to the burdening ports and the number of burdening ports.

The Forwarding Burdened Group Join Delay test follows the group join delay setup with the same addition of burdening ports transmitting meshed unicast traffic, takes a baseline measurement of group join delay, then starts the unicast traffic and reruns the join delay test with the same offered load to the ingress port. The report must give the join delay time in microseconds per egress interface for both the baseline and the burdened response.
sections.plainLanguage: Two more measurements. First, how many different groups can the device keep track of at once. Second, whether the delay grows when the device is also busy copying other people's traffic, which is what a real network looks like.
